title: Your Wallet: Keys and Addresses
objectives: Why your address is safe to share and your seed phrase never is
Where the 12 words come from and what they actually control
How a signature proves you approved something without revealing your key

steps.title: Two halves of a wallet
steps.body:
A <Term id="wallet">wallet</Term> has two halves, and confusing them is how people lose everything.

One is your <Term id="public_key">public key</Term>, written as an <Term id="address">address</Term> - something like `7xKX...9dQ`. It's a destination. Give it to anyone: people use it to send you tokens, exchanges use it to pay you out, sites use it to check what you hold. Publishing it can only bring you things.

The other is your <Term id="private_key">private key</Term>. A 32-byte number nobody ever sees, and it's the only thing that can sign on your wallet's behalf. Whoever holds it controls the address. Not "has access to" - controls. They can empty it in a single transaction, and Solana does not do refunds.

So the mental model worth keeping: **an address is a destination, a private key is a hand.** You hand out destinations all day. You never hand out the hand.

Most people never touch the private key directly. They meet a <Term id="seed_phrase">seed phrase</Term> instead - 12 words, generated once when you install Phantom or Solflare.

**Where the 12 words come from**

The words are not a password stored on a server. They're the root of a tree. From that one sequence your wallet derives every private key and every address you'll ever use, in a fixed order, on any device.

Which cuts both ways, and it's worth saying plainly. Lose the words and you lose the wallet - there is no reset. Leak the words and you've given the wallet away, because anyone can rebuild it on their own phone in about ten seconds.

Three habits that prevent most losses:
- Paper or metal. Never a screenshot, never Notes, never a cloud drive - those sync, and so does the thief.
- No site, no Discord form, no "support agent" needs them. Ever.
- A real wallet will never ask you to re-enter your seed phrase to approve something. If a page asks, close the tab.

steps.title: What a signature actually is
steps.body:
Solana uses Ed25519, an elliptic curve. When you approve something, your wallet combines your private key with the exact bytes of the transaction and produces a <Term id="signature">signature</Term> - 64 bytes of it.

Two properties make that useful. Anyone can check the signature against your <Term id="public_key">public key</Term> and confirm it came from your key, without your key ever leaving the extension. And it can't be reversed - you can't get the key from the signature.

It also means the signature only approves *this specific* transaction. Not your wallet, not a permission, not future transactions. Which is exactly why a drainer has to talk you into approving something new every single time.

questions.prompt: Which of these is safe to share publicly with someone sending you tokens?
questions.explainRight: Your address. That is what it is for.
questions.explainWrong: Only the address. A seed phrase or a private key is complete control of the wallet.

questions.prompt: If a website asks you to enter your seed phrase to 'verify your wallet' or 'claim an airdrop', what should you do?
options: Enter it quickly before the airdrop expires
Close the tab immediately. No legitimate app ever asks for your seed phrase
Send it to a support agent on Telegram
questions.explainRight: Close it. Nobody running a real protocol needs your words to verify anything.
questions.explainWrong: Never. A real wallet never asks for the words, so whoever is asking is taking the wallet.
